article.overview:
A radio science experiment measures the Moon by using radio signals. A spacecraft orbiting the Moon is pulled by the lunar gravity field, so its speed and path change slightly from place to place. Those changes shift the frequency of the radio carrier between the spacecraft and a ground station on Earth (the Doppler effect), and they change the time the signal takes to travel (range). By fitting a model of the spacecraft's motion to these measurements, scientists estimate the coefficients of a spherical-harmonic description of the lunar gravity field [1][4].

The technique has a long lunar history. During the Apollo era, the command and service module's existing S-band transponder was tracked to map large gravity anomalies called mascons [8]. Clementine, Lunar Prospector, SELENE (Kaguya) and GRAIL each extended the method. GRAIL used a dedicated ranging system between two orbiters in 2012 [2][5]. The sources read do not describe a radio science payload operating on the lunar surface, so this article treats the payload class as an orbital and Earth-based measurement system.
article.description:
A radio science experiment is rarely a separate box. It is usually a set of functions spread across three elements: the spacecraft's telecommunications subsystem (transponders, antennas and, for some missions, a stable oscillator), the ground stations of a deep-space network, and the orbit-determination and gravity-processing software on the ground. The ODE description of the Clementine experiment states that the spacecraft's telecom subsystem formed part of the radio science instrument, and that the rest of the instrument sat at NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) ground stations, with much of the equipment shared with routine telecommunications [3].

The ODE page distinguishes two kinds of radio science. Radio tracking derives the magnitude and direction of the Moon's gravity field from Doppler and ranging measurements. Radio propagation attributes modulation of the received signal to the intervening medium, for example during radio occultations by the lunar limb or bistatic radar scattering from the lunar surface [3]. This article concentrates on tracking.

Lunar missions used different radio configurations:

- **Apollo:** S-band tracking of the command and service module, the lunar module and subsatellites [8].
- **Lunar Prospector:** S-band Doppler and ranging, tracked by DSN stations at Goldstone (California), Canberra (Australia) and Madrid (Spain) [4].
- **SELENE (Kaguya):** four-way Doppler through the relay sub-satellite Rstar, plus differential VLBI using X-band radio sources carried on Rstar and Vstar [1].
- **GRAIL:** Ka-band ranging between two orbiters through the Lunar Gravity Ranging System (LGRS), with DSN Doppler tracking [2][5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose is to determine the lunar gravity field and, from it, the distribution of mass inside the Moon. Gravity anomalies record density variations in the crust and upper mantle, and the mascons first recognised in orbital tracking are the best-known example [8]. A higher-resolution gravity field also supports lunar geodesy, the measurement of the Moon's shape, orientation and gravity.

Resolution has grown with each mission. The Lunar Prospector model LP100J is a 100th-degree-and-order solution that used all Lunar Prospector Doppler and range data through 8 February 1999 [4]. The Kaguya SGM100g model is also degree and order 100 and was built from one year of Kaguya tracking data combined with earlier tracking, according to a 2009 conference abstract [9]. The GRAIL data support regional solutions that Goossens et al. evaluate at 0.15° × 0.15°, equivalent to degree and order 1199 [6]. Those GRAIL results are discussed in Scientific Importance.

Radio propagation experiments, such as occultation and bistatic radar measurements, are part of the Clementine record [3]. They are not discussed further here because the sources read give no numerical specifications for them.
article.operating_principle:
**Doppler tracking.** When a spacecraft moves relative to a ground station, the received carrier frequency differs from the transmitted frequency in proportion to the line-of-sight velocity. Small velocity changes caused by the Moon's gravity appear as tiny frequency residuals. Lunar Prospector Doppler was sampled at 1 s and compressed to 10 s for analysis, while most historic Doppler was recorded at 60 s. Historic Doppler noise ranged from 0.3 mm/s to several mm/s, and Clementine DSN data noise was 0.25 mm/s [4].

**Ranging.** Ranging measures the signal's travel time, which gives the distance between the spacecraft and the station. Lunar Prospector data combined Doppler and ranging observations [4].

**Relay configuration.** The ODE page states that the Kaguya relay sub-satellite Rstar was positioned behind the Moon relative to the main orbiter. Rstar therefore carried Doppler and range links between the main orbiter and the Usuda Deep Space Center, and supported four-way Doppler through that relay [1].

**Inter-satellite ranging.** The GRAIL LGRS measures inter-satellite range and its derivative between the twin orbiters [2]. The Goossens et al. analysis uses these data as Ka-band range-rate (KBRR) observations with noise of 0.03 to 0.05 µm/s [6]. Mass anomalies beneath one orbiter perturb the separation between the two spacecraft, and the perturbation is recorded in the range-rate data.

**VLBI.** The Kaguya VRAD experiment measures angular distances between two radio sources (VRAD-1 and VRAD-2) carried on Rstar and Vstar and the distance to quasars, using differential VLBI. Combined with Doppler and ranging data, this is intended to improve the lunar gravitational spherical-harmonic coefficients [1]. The ODE page states an X-band carrier of 8.4 GHz, a 2000 km ground VLBI baseline, a phase-delay accuracy of 3.3 ps and an angular-distance accuracy of 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ (1.1 × 10⁻⁴ arcsec), which it describes as about 20 cm on the Moon [1]. These are instrument values as stated on that page; they were not checked against the JAXA format document.
article.scientific_importance:
Radio science gives the lunar gravity field at a scale that imaging and topography alone cannot provide, because gravity responds to the integrated effect of subsurface density. Lunar Prospector's LP100J solution has a free-air gravity error of about 20 mGal on the equatorial near side and more than 100 mGal for far-side short-wavelength mascon features. The geoid error is about 4 m on the near side and about 30 m on the far side [4]. The far-side error is much larger, and this is why SELENE's relay configuration was designed to observe the far side [1].

The GRAIL mission produced high-resolution gravity solutions from ranging between two orbiters. Goossens et al. (2021) describe patched local solutions from GRAIL Ka-band data with a map resolution of 0.15° × 0.15°, equivalent to degree and order 1199. In their starting-model comparison, the initial adjustment RMS was 30.85 mGal and fell to 5.75 mGal after iteration, against 137 mGal RMS for the GRGM1200A starting model at full resolution. The authors also report a topography correlation of 0.9 reached at local degree 764, compared with 725 for the starting model [6]. These are the authors' own results and have not been independently reproduced in the sources read.

The Apollo 14 and 15 S-band analyses reported detailed gravity profiles of the Serenitatis and Crisium mascons from low-altitude command-module tracking. The results suggested that the mascons are near-surface features [8]. This is an abstract-level finding and should be read with that limitation in mind.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a radio science experiment. Its hardware is usually the spacecraft's existing telecommunications system plus equipment at ground stations, so mass, size and power are rarely published for the radio science function alone. The examples below describe specific missions. They used different bands, spacecraft and tracking networks, and they are not directly comparable.

details.type: Historical flown lunar orbital experiment (Apollo 14 and 15 command and service module, lunar module and subsatellites; Apollo 15 and 16 subsatellite data later used in gravity solutions [4][8]).
details.hardware: The experiment used the existing S-band transponder that served real-time navigation, and the source states that it needed no special hardware [8].
details.measurement: Precision Doppler tracking of the command and service module, the lunar module and the subsatellite [8].
details.mass_dimensions_and_power: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
details.status: Flown. The results were analysed in the early 1970s, and the source for the Apollo 15 analysis is abstract-level metadata only [8].

details.measurements: Radio tracking (Doppler and ranging) and radio propagation [3].
details.tracking_details: Clementine data were recorded at a 10 s count interval, and Clementine DSN data noise was 0.25 mm/s. The Lunar Prospector dataset label notes a Clementine periapse altitude of 415 km [4].
details.bands_frequencies_dates_and_mass: Not stated on the ODE page read [3].

details.tracking: S-band Doppler and ranging, tracked by DSN stations at Goldstone, Canberra and Madrid [4].
details.data_span: 11 January 1998 to 8 February 1999. The nominal mission was about one year. An extended mission at about 30 km average altitude was planned through the end of July 1999. The label does not confirm whether the extended phase was completed [4].
details.models: LP75D (preliminary 75th degree and order, using data to 17 February 1998), LP75G (75th degree and order, using data to 12 April 1998) and LP100J (100th degree and order, using data to 8 February 1999) [4].
details.observation_statistics: LP100J comprises 2,969,982 observations in total, of which 2,589,003 are from Lunar Prospector, in 491 arcs. Post-fit residual RMS was near 1 mm/s [4].
details.mass: Not stated in the sources read.

details.components: RSAT used the relay sub-satellite Rstar with RSAT-1 and RSAT-2 transponders on Rstar and the main orbiter, providing four-way Doppler among the main orbiter, Rstar and Usuda, and two-way range and Doppler between Rstar and Usuda [1]. VRAD used artificial radio sources on Rstar and Vstar, and quasars, for differential VLBI [1].
details.specifications_as_stated_on_the_ode_page: X-band carrier 8.4 GHz; sensitivity stated as 0.17 rad (10 degrees); 2000 km ground VLBI baseline; phase-delay accuracy 3.3 ps; angular-distance accuracy 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ (1.1 × 10⁻⁴ arcsec); equivalent accuracy about 20 cm on the Moon [1].
details.data: Kaguya tracking from 20 October 2007 to 30 October 2008, combined with earlier tracking, produced the SGM100g model of degree and order 100 [9].
details.mass_and_power: Not stated in the sources read.

details.type: Flown lunar orbital experiment on two spacecraft.
details.spacecraft: GRAIL-A and GRAIL-B, renamed Ebb and Flow in January 2012. Each was launched on 10 September 2011 on a Delta-2 2920-10 from Cape Canaveral. GRAIL-A reached lunar orbit on 31 December 2011 and GRAIL-B on 1 January 2012 [5].
details.mass: Dry mass 202 kg and launch mass 307 kg for each spacecraft, as whole-spacecraft values [5].
details.orbit: Near-polar, near-circular science orbit at a mean altitude of 55 km, with a spacecraft separation of 175 to 225 km [5]. The Goossens et al. analysis gives orbit altitudes of about 50 km in the primary mission and about 23 km, then 11 to 20 km after 11 November 2012, in the extended mission [6]. These values disagree and are listed as an evidence gap.
details.instrument: LGRS is a Ka-band ranging instrument based on the GRACE instrument. Its components are an ultra-stable oscillator (USO), a microwave assembly (MWA), a time-transfer assembly (TTA) and a gravity recovery processor assembly (GPA) [2][5]. Frequency bands and ranging precision are not given on the ODE page read [2].
details.end_of_mission: The spacecraft were deliberately impacted on the Moon on 17 December 2012 [5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the radio science function in the sources read. No dimensions were found for the GRAIL LGRS hardware, the Kaguya RSAT and VRAD transponders or the Lunar Prospector radio system.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for the radio science function alone. ESA's eoportal gives a dry mass of 202 kg and a launch (fuelled) mass of 307 kg for each GRAIL spacecraft. These are whole-spacecraft values, not LGRS values [5].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources read. Radio science operations draw on the spacecraft power system, which the sources read do not describe for the radio science function.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Radio tracking needs line of sight between the spacecraft and a DSN station. The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, so the far side is not visible from Earth and direct tracking is interrupted there. The consequence is visible in the Lunar Prospector label, where far-side geoid error is about 30 m compared with about 4 m on the near side [4]. SELENE's relay was introduced to address this geometry [1].

Orbit geometry sets the sensitivity. GRAIL required a low, near-polar and near-circular orbit so that the twin orbiters could measure small perturbations between them [2][5]. The GRAIL LGRS used an ultra-stable oscillator, but the sources read do not quantify its stability [2].

Tracking data depend on ground processing. The ODE page states that GRAIL raw data were collected by the DSN and processed by the GRAIL Science Data System at JPL. The GRAIL radio science data set includes DSN Doppler tracking, open-loop data and media calibrations [2]. The sources read do not quantify the spacecraft thermal, power or non-gravitational force environment for the radio science function.
article.limitations:
Radio tracking measures gravity indirectly, through the effect of the gravity field on spacecraft motion. Resolution depends on orbit altitude, spacecraft geometry and the amount and quality of tracking data [4][6]. The Lunar Prospector label shows that noise and residuals vary widely between data sets, and that far-side errors are much larger than near-side errors [4].

Earth-based tracking cannot see the far side directly. Relay and inter-satellite configurations can reduce that gap, but each has its own coverage and geometry limits [1][2].

The GRAIL results are presented by the authors who produced them, and the Goossens et al. comparisons use a specific starting model and processing choice [6]. Radio science data also depend heavily on the mission's orbit determination, and the sources read do not give a general error budget.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Radio science experiments are normally integrated into an orbiter's telecommunications system and operated through ground stations rather than deployed as separate hardware. This section discusses orbiter-based radio science, which is the basis of every example read. No lunar-surface radio science payload was found in the sources read. A surface radio beacon or navigation transponder would be a different payload (entries 174 and 175).
transportation_process: Earth integration: the transponder, antenna and any oscillator are integrated into the spacecraft telecommunications subsystem, and tracking is scheduled on the DSN. The sources read do not describe the integration steps in detail.
Launch: GRAIL launched on 10 September 2011 on a Delta-2 2920-10 from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station [5].
Lunar transfer and orbit insertion: GRAIL-A reached lunar orbit on 31 December 2011 and GRAIL-B on 1 January 2012 [5].
Science phase: the GRAIL twin orbiters operated in a near-polar orbit at a mean altitude of 55 km, with a separation of 175 to 225 km [5].
Operations: the DSN tracked the orbiters, and the LGRS data were processed at JPL [2].
End of mission: the spacecraft were deliberately impacted on the Moon on 17 December 2012 [5].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The radio science hardware is not deployed as a separate device in the sources read. The Kaguya sub-satellites Rstar and Vstar were placed in lunar orbit to act as relay and VLBI sources [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo command and service module and subsatellite tracking; Lunar Prospector DSN tracking; Clementine tracking; the Kaguya Rstar and Vstar relay configuration; and the GRAIL twin-orbiter ranging system [1][2][4][8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is claimed. The sources read do not provide interface evidence for any surface or lander integration of a radio science payload.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo-era S-band tracking of command and service modules established that orbital radio tracking could reveal mascons. Those results remain a foundation for later lunar gravity work [8]. Lunar Prospector and Clementine provided the 100th-degree-and-order solutions described above, with LP100J using Lunar Prospector data to February 1999 [4]. Kaguya's Rstar and Vstar configuration added a relay and VLBI approach aimed at far-side coverage and at improving the gravity model [1][9]. GRAIL's twin-orbiter ranging produced high-resolution gravity solutions, which Goossens et al. evaluate in their 2021 paper [5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Apollo:** The Apollo S-band results are taken from abstract-level search metadata and a provisional analysis. The mascon interpretation is not checked against the full text [8].
- **Kaguya:** The RSAT and VRAD values come from the ODE instrument page and were not checked against JAXA's format document. The SGM100g model is taken from a 2009 conference abstract that was not read in full [1][9].
- **Clementine:** The ODE page does not state frequencies, mission dates or numerical specifications [3].
- **Lunar Prospector:** The sources read give no radio hardware mass, power or band assignment for the radio system [4].
- **GRAIL:** Orbit altitude values disagree between the ESA summary (mean 55 km) and the Goossens et al. analysis (about 50 km, then 23 km and 11 to 20 km in the extended mission) [5][6]. The ODE page does not give LGRS frequency bands or ranging precision [2]. The end-of-primary and extended mission dates were not verified from primary NASA pages.
- **Goossens et al.:** The patched-solution results and their comparisons are the authors' own and were not independently reproduced [6].
- **Chinese radio science literature:** A 2014 review of Chang'e radio science was located, but its publisher page shows a retraction notice. It is not relied on in this article.
- **Image:** The PIA16493 image is a mission graphic. Reuse conditions were not checked in full, and the full-resolution TIFF was not downloaded [7].
- **Lander compatibility:** No evidence was found for any surface or lander integration of a radio science payload.
- **Lunar location recommendations:** Deferred by the user and not included.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed; scheme, host and path preserved. No URL in this file contains a query string or fragment.

data_quality_notes: Example 1 (Apollo S-band transponder experiment) rests on abstract-level search metadata and a provisional analysis; the mascon interpretation was not checked against the full text.
The SGM100g Kaguya model (reference 9) is taken from a 2009 conference abstract that was not read in full.
Kaguya RSAT and VRAD numerical values are as stated on the ODE instrument page and were not checked against the JAXA format document.

GRAIL orbit altitudes conflict: eoportal gives a mean science-orbit altitude of 55 km, while Goossens et al. give about 50 km in the primary mission and about 23 km, then 11 to 20 km, in the extended mission. Both are reported; neither is preferred.

The eoportal page gives the GRAIL-B lunar orbit insertion date as 'Jan. 01.2011', which is treated as 1 January 2012 because the same page gives GRAIL-A as 31 December 2011 and the mission launched in 2011.
The ODE Clementine page gives no frequencies, mission dates or numerical specifications, and the Clementine dates were not verified from another source.
The Lunar Prospector dataset label gives no radio hardware mass, power or band assignment.
A 2014 Chinese review of Chang'e radio science (Journal of Deep Space Exploration) was located. Its publisher page shows a retraction notice, so it is neither cited nor relied upon.
The GRAIL LGRS frequency bands and ranging precision were not found on the ODE page read; the ODE page refers to Software Interface Specification documents that were not read.
The Goossens et al. (2021) patched-solution results and comparisons are the authors' own and were not independently reproduced.
No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility evidence was found for a radio science payload; none is claimed.
Image PIA16493 is a mission graphic, not a hardware photograph. Its full-resolution TIFF is listed on the source page but was not downloaded, and reuse conditions were not checked in full.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
